newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: SINGAPORE OPL BUNKERING DOWN AFTER PORT LIMIT MOVE.
newsitem.headline: SINGAPORE OPL BUNKERING DOWN AFTER PORT LIMIT MOVE.

text.p: The number of ships refuelling at sea off Singapore has plummetted since the authorties extended the port limits in July, industry sources said on Wednesday.
"The number of ships bunkering off-port-limit (OPL) has dropped to a quarter," one bunker supplier said.
Industry sources estimate the OPL bunkering volume, including ship-to-ship transfers, at about three million tonnes in 1996.

As a result of the sharp drop in OPL bunkering, the amount of fuel lifted in Singapore is expected to rise in the second half of the year as most of the ships that were refuelling at sea now had no choice but to enter the port.
"Not many ships have an alternative, especially in the fourth quarter when the weather in South Korea is really bad and daylight is short because of winter," a major bunker seller said.
Ships were refuelling outside Singapore because they did not have to pay port charges and incur delays related to entering a port, the sources said.
Shipowners save between US$3,000 and US$5,000 by refuelling outside the port limits.
Official bunker sales in the first half of 1997 fell three percent to 8.651 million tonnes from the first half of 1996, latest figures from the Singapore Maritime and Port Authority (MPA) showed.
A similar three-percent drop was recorded in 1996, with bunker sales at 16.9 million tonnes.
In an effort to reverse this trend, the MPA extended the port limt and revised its port charges.
The port limits was extended on the southern and eastern seaboards by between one and three miles on July 11 and the shipping commnunity was informed of the change on July 25.

The new port limits left the shipowners with very little space to refuel at sea, pushed against the traffic separation zone, the highway for ships passing through the Malacca Straits to the South China Sea.
"The western OPL is now squeezed to an alley space and a lot of people are fighting to refuel there. It is very congested," one bunker supplier said.
Shipowners are also being encouraged to take fuel from Singapore through faster port clearance and documentation as well as concessionary port dues for vessels that enter the port solely to bunker.
The concessionary port dues of $1 per 100 gross tonnes (GT), which originally applied to vessels bigger than 50,000 GT, has been reduced to include vessels of 30,000 GT, the sources said.
They said that aside from the Singapore moves, recent boardings by the Indonesian authorities of vessels refuelling in their waters has also deterred ships from refuelling at sea.
As it is not very clear where the international waters are between Singapore and Indonesia, the shipowners and bunker operators are not taking any chance after the recent incidents, the sources said.
In July, the Indonesian authorities boarded several tankers refuelling in its waters.
"We are refraining from doing OPL," one independent bunker supplier said.
